Throughout this post d∈N {d\in\mathbb{N}}d∈N will be a fixed dimension constant. Recall that the k {k}k-th Littlewood-Paley "projection'' of f∈S(Rd) {f\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}f∈S(Rd), k∈Z {k\in\mathbb{Z}}k∈Z, is defined as

Pkf=(φkf^)∨,\displaystyle P_{k}f=(\varphi_{k}\hat{f})^{\vee},Pk​f=(φk​f^​)∨,

where φk(ξ)=φ0(2−kξ) {\varphi_{k}(\xi)=\varphi_{0}(2^{-k}\xi)}φk​(ξ)=φ0​(2−kξ), φ0(ξ)=ψ(ξ)−ψ(2ξ) {\varphi_{0}(\xi)=\psi(\xi)-\psi(2\xi)}φ0​(ξ)=ψ(ξ)−ψ(2ξ) and ψ {\psi}ψ s a C∞ {C^{\infty}}C∞ bump function supported in B(0,2) {B(0,2)}B(0,2) and equals 1 {1}1 in B(0,1) {B(0,1)}B(0,1) in the frequency space. These operators are frequency localisation operators, where each piece Pkf {P_{k}f}Pk​f of f {f}f is localised to frequency ∼2k {\sim2^{k}}∼2k, since the Fourier support of Pkf {P_{k}f}Pk​f is precisely the annulus Ann(2k−1,2k) {\text{Ann}(2^{k-1},2^{k})}Ann(2k−1,2k). The purpose of this post is to see some applications of frequency localisation, in particular in understanding derivatives.

There are three basic interconnected heuristics that one should keep in mind about the frequency localisation of a function, in particular Littlewood-Paley pieces {Pkf}k∈Z {\{P_{k}f\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}}{Pk​f}k∈Z​:

  • Localisation to frequency ∼2k {\sim2^{k}}∼2k basically distroys all the spatial information under scale ∼2−k {\sim2^{-k}}∼2−k. More precisely, Pkf {P_{k}f}Pk​f essentially ocsillates like the plaine wave e2kix {e^{2^{k}ix}}e2kix, and also differentiating Pkf {P_{k}f}Pk​f in the spacial variable mainly amplifies itself by a factor of 2k {2^{k}}2k, c.f. Lemma 6.
  • Different Pkf {P_{k}f}Pk​f are "almost orthogonal'' to each other. In fact, the Pkf {P_{k}f}Pk​f and Plf {P_{l}f}Pl​f are exactly L2 {L^{2}}L2-orthogonal whenever ∣k−l∣>1 {|k-l|>1}∣k−l∣>1. c.f. Theorem 7 Littlewood Paley inequality.
  • For a frequency localised function such as Pkf {P_{k}f}Pk​f, lower Lp {L^{p}}Lp norms control higher Lq {L^{q}}Lq norms. This is analogous to the case of spatial localised function (i.e. functions that has compact support), for which the control is reversed, by the merit of Hölder's inequality. c.f. Lemma 8 Bernstein's inequality, or the closely related Young's convolution inequality, which will be the ultimate source of varous embedding inequalities.
